title: A Tooth Reveals T. rex Ran Hot — Nearly as Warm as You
summary:
For over a century, paleontologists have pieced together T. rex from bones and footprints. Now they've done something that once sounded impossible: they've taken its temperature. The answer — about 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 Celsius) — is shockingly close to our own.

The discovery comes from an unlikely thermometer: fossilized tooth enamel. Inside enamel, rare isotopes of carbon and oxygen can bond together. More bonds form in cooler conditions, fewer in warmer ones. That ratio acts like a chemical thermostat locked inside the tooth.

"No one's been able to make a temperature measurement like this before," said Robert Eagle, a UCLA geobiologist and co-author of the study, published Sept. 16 in Science Advances. "We found T. rex was 36 Celsius, about the same as humans."

Getting there wasn't easy. The original method, developed about a decade ago, needed more fossil material than any museum would sacrifice. So the team refined it, pressurizing the gas sample to get readable measurements from tiny amounts. That convinced the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County to donate small bits of two teeth from "Thomas the T. rex," one of its most complete skeletons.

For comparison, modern reptiles sit around 82–86°F, while birds — dinosaurs' living descendants — run hot at 104–109°F. T. rex landed in between, closer to a mammal.

Why does this matter? A warm body means a fast metabolism, which fits an active predator that could thrive in cold regions like Alaska. T. rex was still a scaly, egg-laying reptile — but it was built to keep moving.
why_it_matters: This matters beyond one dinosaur: chemistry can now pull hard numbers — body temperature, and by extension metabolism — out of fossils that museums once refused to let anyone damage, which could change how scientists model how extinct animals lived and moved. It also sharpens the long-running debate about when warm-bloodedness evolved in the lineage that eventually produced birds.

background_read: T. rex — short for Tyrannosaurus rex, a massive meat-eating dinosaur that lived in North America at the end of the Cretaceous Period — has been dug up and studied by paleontologists for well over a century.
UCLA (the University of California, Los Angeles, a large public university in California) is the home of Robert Eagle, the geobiologist quoted in this study.
The temperature trick he used is called 'clumped isotope' thermometry: scientists first developed it to read temperatures out of minerals, and later applied it to fossil shells, eggs and teeth.
Science Advances (a peer-reviewed journal published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the same organization behind the journal Science) printed the results.

Whether dinosaurs were warm-blooded has been one of paleontology's longest arguments, and because birds are dinosaurs' living descendants and really do run hot, many scientists suspected the biggest dinosaurs did too — this tooth adds hard evidence to that side.

perspectives.description: For paleontologists this is a new window into how dinosaurs actually worked. A temperature near a mammal's supports the picture of T. rex as an active, fast-moving hunter that could survive cold places like Alaska. The refined method also needs only tiny samples, so far more museum specimens become testable.

The result rests on small bits of two teeth from a single skeleton, 'Thomas the T. rex', so it may describe that individual more than the whole species. Isotope-based temperatures also come with error ranges, and some researchers are cautious about pushing the technique so confidently into deep time.

Historically, this fits a decades-long shift in how dinosaurs are portrayed — from slow, cold-blooded lizards to active, warm-blooded animals. It is one more data point in an argument that has swung back and forth for decades, and it does not by itself prove that every dinosaur ran hot.

The obvious next step is to run the same test on more dinosaurs of different sizes and climates, and on the earliest ancestors of birds. That could build a temperature curve for the whole family tree, letting scientists test ideas about how dinosaurs grew, moved and coped with changing climates.
